titleEn: The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect
author: Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie
introFa: کتاب «The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect» نوشته Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Why Freud? Why now? These are easy questions to ask when faced with Élizabeth Roudinesco’s new book, Freud: In His Time and Ours. It is easy to dismiss Freud for his failings: a seemingly overt misogyny, participation in a class system from which he greatly benefitted, lack of foresight for the coming horror of the Nazi regime, to name a few. Roudinesco’s biography deftly defends his shortcomings by demonstrating the brilliance of the man and his work. Roudinesco’s text is also smart because it leaves out the conclusions, thus avoiding simplistic parallels or too narrowly focused or time- sensitive assessments. It is a book about Freud in our time, without highlighting specific historical or cultural events. Instead, it speaks to the spirit of the moment in which we are living, a moment, in the United States, of extreme division and political upheaval, cultural revolution, and empowerment of the previously silenced. We can read our cultural moment as one of great disarray, and many want to, but we can also read it as a historical situation in which stand on the precipice of change. To know Freud, as Roudinesco explains him, is to know a man and his theories, all of which center on the ability to transform oneself and one’s life. For Freud, that change could only come via the analytic experience with whose creation he is credited. For our time, perhaps that experience is translatable to social and political movements. As Roudinesco intimates, Freud is a man for “our” time, because he is a man for all times; his meteoric rise to fame, coupled with his status as one the man who plumbed the depths of the mind of modernism, are unquestioned by Roudinesco, as she explores the parallels between the myths that underpin Freud’s theories and the mythic status of Freud himself. Woven throughout the text are consistent references to the literary figures of Oedipus, Hamlet, and Moses, whose stories are the inspirations for Freud’s most famous theories. By intertwining the myths with biographical details of Freud’s own life, Roudinesco effectively makes Freud into a mythic creation himself, from the child born into the specter of Communist thought to the man dying having just escaped Nazi-occupied Austria, and through it all, writing his epic of psychoanalysis. Freud: In His Time and Ours also emphasizes Freud as master of literary arts. Roudinesco points out, early in the book, that “Freud saw himself as Goethe’s heir.” This places Freud not so much as part of a scientific, but more as one of a literary tradition. His work is a merger of natural science and humanities, both pragmatic and fanciful, practical and fictive, a combination that allows Freud the freedom to conceive of the human mind in ways never before attempted, and with accuracy never previously, and for Roudinesco, never subsequently, achieved. The assertion of Freud as a significant literary figure drives the biographer to spend substantial energy on Freud’s early works, especially The Interpretation of Dreams (1899) and the body of work that stems from it, including the theory of sublimation. As Roudinesco points out, for Freud, “the ideal of a ‘civilized morality’ rested not on the preservation of the monogamous family or conjugal fidelity, but on the necessary sublimation of the drives in favor of creative activities.” The literary master of the mind, in this light, sacrificed his actual sex life for his theoretical one, to the great benefit of psychoanalytic development. For although Freud did not actually advocate chastity per se, Freud believed that the sublimation of the sex drive was more satisfying than a temporary sating of it. For those readers at all versed in post- Freudian developments of the discipline, it is easy to see where Lacan picks up Freud’s person and professional experiments in order to form the underpinning of his own work. Interestingly, and partially by necessity to limit an already longish text, Roudinesco leaves out mention of those theorists and practitioners in the Freudian tradition with whom Freud did not directly work or analyze. She even excludes most of the conflicts that arose between Klein and Freud and between Jung and Freud. The exclusion of those details, based more in the specific details and developments of theory than in the actions of daily life, do make the text a bit less weighty for scholars of psychoanalysis, but the omission likely makes it accessible to a general audience. The accessibility of the text is one of its strengths. It could be read by anyone for a refreshing, non-academic journey through Freud’s life and times, with special focus on his interpersonal connections and political beliefs. Roudinesco covertly uses the descriptions of Freud’s relationships with women, both platonic and romantic, to demonstrate a respect and admiration for them that seems aimed at redeeming his reputation as a misogynist. The entire chapter titled “Among Woman” is devoted to Freud’s intersection with women as patients and colleagues. The chapter is not entirely a success in redeeming Freud’s ostensibly sexist views, as Roudinesco is forced to point out, “Freud has remained trapped in a conception of women, femininity and love life that had arisen out of German Romanticism and Naturphilosophie.” Still, if the reader considers the immense influence of Freud’s work and its importance in current intellectual and cultural life, what Roudinesco shows is Freud’s determination to understand female sexuality and use his analytic practice to free women of the strictures placed on their sexual expression through what he considered hysterical symptoms. To a certain extent, Freud recognized was that women were vulnerable to sexual abuses and that such abuse was far more common than discussed. Contemporary society has made relatively little progress in this area. Despite the sexual liberation of women beginning in the 1960s, women are still faced with harassment and violation every day. The exposure of such abuse in the entertainment and media industries is only a tiny inroad into combatting the behavior. Freud’s theories cannot correct these abuses, but they can, in part, explain them, and understanding is part of treatment and prevention. This Freud for our time, as Roudinesco frames him, can also offer to us insight into what happens when a political or religious system approaches absolute power. Texts such as The Future of Illusion (1927), Totem and Taboo (1913), Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1921), and Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) are mentioned but not deeply explored in this biography, but they are all useful for explaining how and why our current political situation devolved into a “shit-hole.” We still need Freud to help us understand how leadership can go widely awry. Freud’s theories offer no solutions for political or social degradation; they do however, give us a better understanding of the causes and effects of such phenomena, and through this knowledge we can act in direct opposition. Freud shows contemporary audiences a path for change. Ultimately, Roudinesco’s text gives readers an entrée into the life and times of Sigmund Freud by connecting the basics of his own personal psychology, his familial ties, professional relationships, and interactions with the professional and political forces contemporary to him. The book is not a traditional biography or scholarly exploration. It is, instead, an enjoyable portrait of one of the most important thinkers of modern society, one whose ideas continue to resonate suggestively today. Gina Masucci MacKenzie is the Associate Dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Holy Family University. Her first book, The Theatre of the Real: Yeats, Beckett, and Sondhiem (2008) explores Lacanian psychoanalysis in modern theater. Her next book, Stage Mothers will examine maternal relationships in twenty-first-century popular musical theater. Gina Masucci MacKenzie Why Freud Now? Freud: In His Time and Ours Élisabeth Roudinesco Catherine Porter, trans.
